tytul: Quick refrigerator cucumber and onion pickles (Mississippi State Extension)
wstep: This card describes the Mississippi State Extension recipe for quick-pickle cucumbers and onions, a refrigerator pickle that keeps for about a week.

akapity: 2 large cucumbers, 1 medium onion, 1 garlic clove, 1 cup white distilled or cider vinegar and 1 cup water.
The brine also has 2 tablespoons sugar, 2 teaspoons salt and 1 teaspoon pepper.
Use only vinegar labelled 5% acidity; white and cider vinegar can be used interchangeably; do not use wine vinegars, homemade vinegar or lemon juice.
Vinegar with less than 5% acidity should never be used in home food preservation.
Do not change the proportions of vinegar, vegetables and water in the recipe.

JarAtlas rule (cautious): do not replace it with a stronger vinegar and do not dilute a stronger vinegar with water yourself; Penn State Extension advises staying within 5–7% acidity for home food preservation and diluting vinegar only when a tested recipe says so.
Wash the cucumbers under running water and slice them thinly.
Peel the onion and cut it into thin slices; cut the garlic into small pieces.
Place the vegetables in a one-quart jar (about 946 ml).
Stir the vinegar, water, sugar, salt and pepper until dissolved, then pour the brine into the jar, making sure the vegetables are covered.
Cover the jar and refrigerate until chilled, or overnight.
The vegetables keep for about a week in the refrigerator.
These pickles are not heat processed, so they are not shelf-stable at room temperature and must be kept in the refrigerator.
Do not decrease the amount of vinegar, because an unsafe product may result; for a milder taste add sugar rather than reduce the vinegar.

JarAtlas rule (cautious): keep the jar on the middle shelf of the refrigerator, not in the door: Wisconsin Extension assumes 40 °F (4.4 °C) or colder for refrigerator pickles, while a Polish sanitary inspection office gives about 10 °C for the door, even though it suggests the door for jars of preserves.
Fresh vegetables are low-acid foods, with a pH above 4.6.
The acid level must be adequate and even throughout the product to prevent the growth of botulism bacteria.
